pitanja.pitanje: What happens on the last line?
pitanja.zanimljivost: $move$ forces the closure to take ownership of everything it uses, even if it only needs a reference. That's essential for threads – the closure may outlive the current function.

pitanja.pitanje: Where does $Box<T>$ store its value?
pitanja.zanimljivost: The box itself is just a pointer on the stack. When it is dropped, the value on the heap is freed too.

pitanja.pitanje: Why does this recursive type need $Box$?
odgovori: Otherwise the size would be infinite
pitanja.zanimljivost: A $Box$ has a known size (one pointer), which breaks the infinite recursion in the type's size.

pitanja.pitanje: What is $Rc<T>$?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Rc stands for Reference Counted. For sharing across threads use $Arc<T>$.

pitanja.pitanje: What does $Rc::clone(&a)$ do?
pitanja.zanimljivost: The Book recommends $Rc::clone(&a)$ over $a.clone()$ so cheap clones are visually distinct from expensive ones.

pitanja.pitanje: When does $RefCell<T>$ check the borrowing rules?
odgovori: At run time – panics if broken
At compile time, like ordinary references
pitanja.zanimljivost: That's interior mutability: you can mutate through $&RefCell<T>$, but $borrow_mut$ twice at once panics.

pitanja.pitanje: What can a cycle of $Rc$ pointers cause, and what's the fix?
pitanja.zanimljivost: In a cycle the strong count never drops to zero. A tree typically uses $Rc$ from parent to child and $Weak$ from child to parent.

pitanja.pitanje: What lets you pass $&String$ where $&str$ is expected?
pitanja.zanimljivost: The compiler inserts as many $deref$ calls as needed at compile time – no run-time cost.

pitanja.pitanje: How do you drop a value before the end of its scope?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Calling the $Drop::drop$ method directly is forbidden, because Rust would call it again at the end of scope (a double free).

pitanja.pitanje: What does $Rc<RefCell<T>>$ give you?
pitanja.zanimljivost: In the Book's mock-object example this lets tests record messages through a shared reference.

pitanja.pitanje: Match each smart pointer with its role
pitanja.zanimljivost: To use a $Weak$, call $upgrade()$ – it returns $Option<Rc<T>>$, since the value might be gone.

pitanja.pitanje: When is the value inside an $Rc$ dropped?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Weak references don't keep the value alive. (The allocation itself stays until the weak count also reaches 0.)

pitanja.pitanje: What does this print?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Each $Rc::clone$ only increments a counter – the 5 itself isn't copied. When $c$ goes out of scope the count drops back. The value is freed when it reaches 0.

pitanja.pitanje: What happens here?
odgovori: It compiles, then panics at run time
$r2$ gets a copy of the vector
pitanja.zanimljivost: $RefCell$ moves the borrowing rules from compile time to run time. $try_borrow_mut$ returns a $Result$ instead of panicking, if you want to handle it.

pitanja.pitanje: What does $.join()$ on a $JoinHandle$ do?
odgovori: Waits for the thread to finish
Merges the thread into the main thread
pitanja.zanimljivost: Rust threads are OS threads (1:1 model), not green threads.

pitanja.pitanje: What happens to spawned threads when $main$ finishes?
pitanja.zanimljivost: That's why the Book's first example sometimes prints only part of the output from the spawned thread.

pitanja.pitanje: What does $mpsc$ stand for?
odgovori: Message passing over a shared channel
pitanja.zanimljivost: You clone the transmitter ($tx$) for several producers, but there's only one receiver ($rx$).

pitanja.pitanje: What happens to a value after $tx.send(val)$?
odgovori: It is copied for both sides
pitanja.zanimljivost: If you try to use $val$ after sending, the compiler stops you – the receiving thread might already be changing it.

pitanja.pitanje: How is a $Mutex$ unlocked in Rust?
odgovori: Only when the thread that locked it exits
pitanja.zanimljivost: $lock()$ returns a $MutexGuard$. You can't forget to unlock – but you can hold the guard too long.

pitanja.pitanje: Why share a $Mutex$ between threads with $Arc$ and not $Rc$?
pitanja.zanimljivost: $Rc$ doesn't implement $Send$, so the compiler won't even let you move it into a thread. Atomics cost a little, so $Rc$ stays for single-threaded code.

pitanja.pitanje: What does it mean that a type is $Sync$?
odgovori: Its $&T$ can be sent to other threads
It must be locked to use
It runs on one thread only
pitanja.zanimljivost: $Send$: ownership can move to another thread. $Sync$: sharing $&T$ between threads is safe. $Rc$ is neither; $Cell$ is $Send$ but not $Sync$.

pitanja.pitanje: What do scoped threads ($thread::scope$, Rust 1.63) allow?
odgovori: Spawning an unlimited number of threads
pitanja.zanimljivost: All threads in the scope are joined before $scope$ returns, so borrowing from the stack is safe.

pitanja.pitanje: Can safe Rust code still deadlock?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Rust prevents data races, but not logic errors like two threads locking two mutexes in opposite order.

pitanja.pitanje: Implementing $Send$ or $Sync$ by hand requires…
pitanja.zanimljivost: They are auto traits: a type made only of $Send$ parts is automatically $Send$.

pitanja.pitanje: Match each tool with its job
pitanja.zanimljivost: Go's motto, quoted in the Book: “Do not communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating.”

pitanja.pitanje: Why doesn't this compile?
pitanja.zanimljivost: The compiler can't know the thread finishes before $v$ is dropped, so it asks for $move ||$. Scoped threads ($thread::scope$) are the other fix – they're guaranteed to end inside the scope.

pitanja.pitanje: What does calling an $async fn$ return?
pitanja.zanimljivost: The body hasn't even started yet – the future is just a description of work to be done.

pitanja.pitanje: What happens to a future that is never awaited or polled?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Futures are lazy, like iterators. The compiler warns about unused futures.

pitanja.pitanje: What does Rust's standard library provide for running futures?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Popular runtimes are $tokio$, $smol$ and $async-std$. The Book uses its own helper crate, $trpl$.

pitanja.pitanje: How is “await” written in Rust?
pitanja.zanimljivost: The postfix form makes chaining easy: $get(url).await?.text().await?$.

pitanja.pitanje: Match each async tool with what it does
pitanja.zanimljivost: Unlike $thread::sleep$, an async sleep doesn't block the whole thread – other tasks keep running.

pitanja.pitanje: Why do some futures need to be pinned ($Pin$)?
odgovori: They always need to stay on the heap
pitanja.zanimljivost: An $async$ block can borrow its own local variables across $.await$; moving it would break those internal pointers.

pitanja.pitanje: How does the Book distinguish concurrency from parallelism?
odgovori: Switching tasks vs. running at once
One CPU core vs. a GPU
pitanja.zanimljivost: One person switching between tasks is concurrency; a team working on tasks simultaneously is parallelism.

pitanja.pitanje: What does $std::thread::sleep$ inside an async task do?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Long blocking work belongs in $spawn_blocking$ or on a separate thread.

pitanja.pitanje: What is a stream in async Rust?
pitanja.zanimljivost: The $Stream$ trait isn't in the standard library yet; it lives in crates like $futures$ and $tokio-stream$.

pitanja.pitanje: How does an executor drive a future forward?
odgovori: By running it on a new thread
Through a callback after each line of code
pitanja.zanimljivost: $poll$ returns $Poll::Ready(value)$ or $Poll::Pending$; in the latter case the future arranges to be woken later.

pitanja.pitanje: Since which Rust version can traits contain $async fn$?
pitanja.zanimljivost: $async/await$ itself arrived in 1.39 (2019); $async fn$ in traits took until the end of 2023.

pitanja.pitanje: What does this program print?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Calling an $async fn$ only creates a future – none of its code runs until something polls it. Without a runtime (Tokio, smol…) or $.await$ the future is just dropped.

pitanja.pitanje: Can a Rust struct inherit fields from another struct?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Instead of inheritance Rust uses composition and traits. The Book argues that inheritance often shares more code than needed.

pitanja.pitanje: What is $Box<dyn Draw>$?
pitanja.zanimljivost: It allows a $Vec$ to hold different types – buttons and text boxes – as long as all implement $Draw$.

pitanja.pitanje: Which method makes a trait unusable as $dyn Trait$?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Methods returning $Self$ or having type parameters break dyn compatibility (formerly “object safety”), since the vtable can't know the concrete type.

pitanja.pitanje: What is a cost of dynamic dispatch?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Generics produce faster but larger code; trait objects produce smaller but slightly slower code.

pitanja.pitanje: How does the Book's $AveragedCollection$ show encapsulation?
odgovori: Private fields keep the average in sync
pitanja.zanimljivost: Since $list$ and $average$ are private, users can't change one without the other.

pitanja.pitanje: In the blog post state pattern, why does $request_review$ take $self: Box<Self>$?
odgovori: Boxed methods are faster to call
pitanja.zanimljivost: Taking ownership of the box makes the old state unusable – each transition returns a brand-new state object.

pitanja.pitanje: What does the Book suggest as a more “Rusty” alternative to the state pattern?
odgovori: Each state is a separate type
Global boolean flags for each of the states
pitanja.zanimljivost: With $DraftPost$ and $PendingReviewPost$, trying to publish a draft is a compile error, not a run-time bug.

pitanja.pitanje: Which is NOT a way to achieve polymorphism in Rust?
pitanja.objasnjenje: Rust has no classes and no inheritance; the other three are all common ways to write code that works with many types.
pitanja.zanimljivost: Enums are the best fit when the set of variants is closed; trait objects when other crates should add new types.

pitanja.pitanje: How big is $&dyn Trait$ on a 64-bit machine?
pitanja.zanimljivost: It's a fat pointer: one pointer to the data and one to the vtable (methods, size, alignment, destructor).

pitanja.pitanje: What does Rust offer in place of inherited method implementations?
pitanja.zanimljivost: A type can implement many traits, so it can pick up default behavior from several sources at once.

pitanja.pitanje: Why can't you write $Box<dyn Dup>$?
pitanja.zanimljivost: A trait object hides the concrete type, so a method returning $Self$ can't be called through it. Adding $where Self: Sized$ to $dup$ excludes just that method and makes the trait „dyn compatible“ again.

pitanja.pitanje: Which of these is NOT one of $unsafe$'s “superpowers”?
pitanja.objasnjenje: Inside $unsafe$ references are still borrow-checked; you just get five extra abilities (also: $unsafe$ traits and $union$ fields).
pitanja.zanimljivost: Keeping $unsafe$ blocks small makes it much easier to find a memory bug: you know where to look.

pitanja.pitanje: Which raw pointer operation requires $unsafe$?
pitanja.zanimljivost: $&raw const x$ or $&x as *const i32$ is safe – a pointer that is never read can't hurt anyone.

pitanja.pitanje: Why does $Iterator$ use an associated type ($type Item$) instead of a generic $Iterator<T>$?
odgovori: Associated types are faster to compile
pitanja.zanimljivost: With $Iterator<T>$ a type could implement it several times and every $next()$ call would need a type annotation.

pitanja.pitanje: How do you call $baby_name$ from trait $Animal$ when $Dog$ has its own one too?
pitanja.zanimljivost: This is fully qualified syntax. It's needed for associated functions without $self$, where the compiler can't infer the type.

pitanja.pitanje: What is the newtype pattern commonly used for?
odgovori: Disabling type checks for a wrapped value
pitanja.zanimljivost: $struct Wrapper(Vec<String>);$ is local, so you may implement $Display$ for it. The wrapper costs nothing at run time.

pitanja.pitanje: What does the never type $!$ describe?
odgovori: A value that is always zero or empty
pitanja.zanimljivost: $panic!$, $continue$, $loop$ without $break$ and $std::process::exit$ all have type $!$, which can coerce to any type.

pitanja.pitanje: What does $type Kilometers = i32;$ create?
pitanja.zanimljivost: You can add $Kilometers$ and plain $i32$ freely. For type safety you'd need a newtype instead.

pitanja.pitanje: What does $?Sized$ in $fn f<T: ?Sized>(t: &T)$ mean?
odgovori: $T$ may be a dynamically sized type
$T$ size is checked at run time
pitanja.zanimljivost: Generics get an implicit $Sized$ bound. $?Sized$ relaxes it so $T$ can be $str$ or $[u8]$ behind a reference.

pitanja.pitanje: What can you pass where an $fn(i32) -> i32$ parameter is expected?
odgovori: Only a boxed closure like $Box<dyn Fn>$
pitanja.zanimljivost: $fn$ (lowercase) is a type, not a trait. Function pointers implement all three closure traits.

pitanja.pitanje: Match each kind of macro with an example
pitanja.zanimljivost: Macros run at compile time and can take a variable number of arguments – something functions can't.

pitanja.pitanje: How do you make $+$ work for your own $Point$ type?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Only operators listed in $std::ops$ can be overloaded – you can't invent new operators.

pitanja.pitanje: What does $trait OutlinePrint: fmt::Display$ mean?
odgovori: It inherits all of $Display$'s method code
pitanja.zanimljivost: $Display$ is a supertrait, so methods of $OutlinePrint$ may call $to_string()$.

pitanja.pitanje: What does this print?
pitanja.zanimljivost: $type$ only gives another name – $Km$ and $i32$ are the same type. For real protection against mixing units use a newtype: $struct Km(i32);$.

pitanja.pitanje: Where do the bytes of a string literal live?
odgovori: In static memory, in the binary
pitanja.zanimljivost: Static memory is loaded together with the program and lives for its whole run – hence the $'static$ lifetime of literals.

pitanja.pitanje: What does $Box::leak$ give you?
odgovori: A raw pointer to free later
pitanja.zanimljivost: Leaking is safe in Rust. It's handy for data created at startup that must live until the program exits.

pitanja.pitanje: With respect to $T$, the type $&'a mut T$ is…
pitanja.zanimljivost: If $&mut$ were covariant, you could store a short-lived reference where a $'static$ one is expected – a classic memory bug.

pitanja.pitanje: Which of these types is contravariant in $T$?
pitanja.zanimljivost: A function that accepts any $&'a str$ is more useful than one that requires $&'static str$ – the subtyping goes “the other way”.

pitanja.pitanje: What is the only legal way to mutate data behind a shared reference?
pitanja.zanimljivost: $Cell$, $RefCell$, $Mutex$ and the atomics are all built on top of $UnsafeCell$.

pitanja.pitanje: How does Gjengset describe a lifetime?
odgovori: A region of code where a reference is valid
The number of stack frames a value survives
pitanja.zanimljivost: A lifetime can have “holes”: a borrow can be invalid for a while and then become valid again.

pitanja.pitanje: In which order are local variables dropped?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Struct fields and tuple elements are the opposite – they're dropped in source order.

pitanja.pitanje: How can you move a value out from behind a $&mut T$?
pitanja.zanimljivost: $mem::take$ leaves $Default::default()$ behind, $mem::replace$ leaves a value you choose. The owner must never see an empty place.

pitanja.pitanje: Which of these types implements $Copy$?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Shared references can be freely copied; an exclusive reference must stay unique, so it can only be moved or reborrowed.

pitanja.pitanje: How does a $static$ item differ from a $const$?
pitanja.zanimljivost: A $const$ is copied into every place it is used, so taking its address twice can give two different pointers.

pitanja.pitanje: Does this compile?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Thanks to non-lexical lifetimes (NLL, 2018), a borrow ends at its last use, not at the end of the block. Add $println!("{r}")$ at the end and it stops compiling.

pitanja.pitanje: What is the size of this struct?
pitanja.zanimljivost: With C layout, fields stay in order: $a$ (1) + 3 padding + $b$ (4) + $c$ (1) + 3 padding so the size is a multiple of the alignment 4.

pitanja.pitanje: Without $#[repr(C)]$, how big would the same $a: u8, b: u32, c: u8$ struct be?
pitanja.zanimljivost: The default Rust layout makes no promises about field order, so the compiler can place $b$ first and pack $a$ and $c$ together.

pitanja.pitanje: What does $#[repr(transparent)]$ guarantee?
odgovori: Same layout as its single field
Fields stay in source order, like $repr(C)$
pitanja.zanimljivost: It allows safely casting between a newtype and the wrapped type, also across FFI.

pitanja.pitanje: What is the risk of $#[repr(packed)]$?
odgovori: Fields get reordered by the compiler
pitanja.zanimljivost: Taking a reference to an unaligned field is undefined behavior, so the compiler forbids it in packed structs.

pitanja.pitanje: What is $size_of::<Option<Box<i32>>>()$ on a 64-bit target?
pitanja.zanimljivost: The niche optimization: a $Box$ can never be null, so $None$ is stored as the null pointer – no extra tag byte needed.

pitanja.pitanje: Which of these is NOT a wide (fat) pointer?
pitanja.objasnjenje: $&u64$ is just an address. Slices carry a length and trait objects a vtable pointer, so those are two words.
pitanja.zanimljivost: The extra word is what lets $len()$ on a slice and method calls on $dyn$ work without looking anything up.

pitanja.pitanje: What is a downside of static dispatch with generics?
odgovori: A copy of the code per type
Slower calls at run time through a vtable
pitanja.zanimljivost: Gjengset suggests a trick: a generic outer function converting to a concrete type and calling a non-generic inner one.

pitanja.pitanje: How does $trait Foo<T>$ differ from a trait with $type T;$?
pitanja.zanimljivost: With a generic trait, the same type can implement $Foo<i32>$ and $Foo<String>$. Associated types make inference easier.

pitanja.pitanje: Is $impl From<MyType> for Vec<i32>$ allowed in your crate?
pitanja.zanimljivost: The orphan rule lets you implement a foreign trait for a foreign type if a local type appears as a trait parameter in the right position.

pitanja.pitanje: What kind of type is $impl Trait$ in a return position?
pitanja.zanimljivost: The concrete type exists and the compiler knows it; the caller only knows it implements the trait.

pitanja.pitanje: What is $size_of::<()>()$?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Zero-sized types are common: $()$, unit structs, $PhantomData<T>$. A $HashSet<T>$ is in fact a $HashMap<T, ()>$.

pitanja.pitanje: How can a trait keep a generic method and still be usable as $dyn Trait$?
odgovori: Give the method a default body
pitanja.zanimljivost: Such a method is left out of the vtable – you just can't call it on a trait object.

pitanja.pitanje: What are $size_of::<A>()$ and $size_of::<B>()$?
pitanja.zanimljivost: In practice Rust reorders $A$ as $u32, u8, u8$ plus 2 bytes of padding. $repr(C)$ keeps the written order: 3 bytes after $a$ so that $b$ is aligned to 4, and 3 more at the end.

pitanja.pitanje: Which is NOT one of Gjengset's four principles for interfaces?
pitanja.objasnjenje: The four are: unsurprising, flexible, obvious and constrained.
pitanja.zanimljivost: “Constrained” is about thinking ahead: everything you expose becomes a promise you must keep.

pitanja.pitanje: Match each naming convention with its meaning
pitanja.zanimljivost: Following these conventions means users can guess what your methods do without reading the docs.

pitanja.pitanje: Why should a library implement $Debug$, $Clone$, $Default$… even if it doesn't need them?
odgovori: The compiler requires it for public types
pitanja.zanimljivost: A user can't write $impl Debug for YourType$ in their crate, so a missing derive forces awkward wrappers.

pitanja.pitanje: Why is adding a blanket implementation to a public trait usually a breaking change?
odgovori: It may conflict with users' impls
pitanja.zanimljivost: Even adding an ordinary trait impl can break code if method names become ambiguous.

pitanja.pitanje: What does $#[non_exhaustive]$ on a public enum do?
pitanja.zanimljivost: It lets you add variants later in a minor version. On structs it prevents users from constructing them with literal syntax.

pitanja.pitanje: What is a sealed trait?
odgovori: One that other crates can't implement
One whose methods are all $unsafe$ to call
pitanja.zanimljivost: The trick: the trait has a supertrait in a private module, which outsiders can't name.

pitanja.pitanje: Why take $impl AsRef<Path>$ instead of $&Path$?
pitanja.zanimljivost: That's why $File::open("x.txt")$ works with a plain string literal.

pitanja.pitanje: What does a typestate API like $Rocket<Grounded>$ / $Rocket<Launched>$ achieve?
odgovori: States are checked at run time
pitanja.zanimljivost: The state parameter is usually a zero-sized $PhantomData$, so it costs nothing at run time.

pitanja.pitanje: What does $#[must_use]$ do?
odgovori: Warns if the return value is ignored
Panics if the value is dropped
pitanja.zanimljivost: $Result$ and all iterator adapters are marked $#[must_use]$.

pitanja.pitanje: Why can re-exposing a dependency's type in your public API be risky?
odgovori: It makes the compiled crate larger
pitanja.zanimljivost: If users get a $Bytes$ from your crate and $bytes$ releases 2.0, upgrading it breaks your users too.

pitanja.pitanje: What happens to code examples in $///$ doc comments?
odgovori: They are only syntax-highlighted in HTML
They are compiled but never run
pitanja.zanimljivost: Lines starting with $#$ are hidden in the rendered docs but still compiled – handy for setup code.

pitanja.pitanje: Why take $impl Into<String>$ here?
pitanja.zanimljivost: A $String$ argument is moved in without copying, and a $&str$ is converted only when needed. The cost: a generic function is compiled once per type it's used with.

pitanja.pitanje: Which two kinds of error representation does Gjengset compare?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Enumerated: an enum the caller can match on. Opaque: one type (like a $Box<dyn Error>$) with a message.

pitanja.pitanje: Which traits must a type implement to be $std::error::Error$?
pitanja.zanimljivost: $Error$ itself has no required methods – just these two supertraits.

pitanja.pitanje: What is $Error::source()$ for?
odgovori: Finding the file and line of the error
pitanja.zanimljivost: Following $source()$ repeatedly gives a chain of errors – e.g. “config failed” ← “read failed” ← “permission denied”.

pitanja.pitanje: Why should opaque errors usually be $Send + Sync$?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Errors are often returned from a thread pool or an async task running on another thread.

pitanja.pitanje: How does $?$ convert one error type into another?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Implement $From<io::Error> for MyError$ and $?$ works on I/O results in your functions.

pitanja.pitanje: Match each crate with its typical use
pitanja.zanimljivost: Both crates were written by David Tolnay, who also wrote $serde$, $syn$ and $quote$.

pitanja.pitanje: Why should an error type be $'static$?
odgovori: So it lives in the binary
So it can be a constant
pitanja.zanimljivost: Downcasting ($downcast_ref::<io::Error>()$) is built on $Any$, which only works for $'static$ types.

pitanja.pitanje: Rust's API guidelines say error messages ($Display$) should be…
pitanja.zanimljivost: Messages are often chained together (“failed to read config: no such file”), so short lowercase fragments read best.

pitanja.pitanje: A lookup simply finds nothing. What is the idiomatic return?
pitanja.zanimljivost: “Not found” is often a normal outcome, not an error – e.g. $HashMap::get$ returns $Option$.

pitanja.pitanje: How do you use $?$ on an $Option$ in a function returning $Result$?
pitanja.zanimljivost: $ok_or_else$ builds the error lazily. The opposite direction is $.ok()?$.

pitanja.pitanje: What does $JoinHandle::join$ return if the thread panicked?
odgovori: It blocks forever, waiting for the thread
pitanja.zanimljivost: A panic in one thread doesn't bring down the whole program – unless it's the main thread, or $panic = 'abort'$ is set.

pitanja.pitanje: Why does $?$ work on both lines?
pitanja.zanimljivost: There's a blanket $impl From<E: Error> for Box<dyn Error>$. Libraries usually prefer their own error enum (often via $thiserror$), while applications like $anyhow::Error$.

pitanja.pitanje: Cargo features should be…
pitanja.zanimljivost: Enabling a feature should only add things, never remove or change behavior that others rely on.

pitanja.pitanje: What does Cargo create for an optional dependency?
pitanja.zanimljivost: The $dep:name$ syntax (Rust 1.60) lets you hide that implicit feature and expose a nicer name.

pitanja.pitanje: What is feature unification?
odgovori: Each crate gets the union of all requests
Each dependent gets its own separately built copy
pitanja.zanimljivost: If two crates in the dependency graph enable different features of $tokio$, it's built once with both.

pitanja.pitanje: What is the $[patch]$ section of $Cargo.toml$ for?
odgovori: Applying $.diff$ files to the source code
pitanja.zanimljivost: Handy for testing a fix in a dependency (e.g. from a git branch) before it's released.

pitanja.pitanje: What does the $rust-version$ field in $Cargo.toml$ declare?
odgovori: The newest release the crate was tested on
pitanja.zanimljivost: MSRV is a promise to users on older compilers. Since Rust 1.84 the resolver can prefer dependency versions compatible with it.

pitanja.pitanje: What does $#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]$ do?
odgovori: Compiles the item only on Linux
Checks the OS at run time
pitanja.zanimljivost: $cfg!(…)$ (the macro) evaluates to a $bool$ instead – but both branches must compile everywhere.

pitanja.pitanje: What do $lto = true$ and $codegen-units = 1$ trade?
pitanja.zanimljivost: With more codegen units the compiler works in parallel but sees less of the program at once, missing some optimizations.

pitanja.pitanje: In $Cargo.toml$, what does $serde = "1.0"$ allow?
pitanja.zanimljivost: It's a caret requirement ($^1.0$): updates that semver promises are compatible. $=1.0.0$ pins an exact version.

pitanja.pitanje: How can you optimize dependencies while your own crate stays unoptimized in dev builds?
odgovori: A profile override for other packages
Build everything twice with different flags
pitanja.zanimljivost: $[profile.dev.package."*"] opt-level = 3$ – the dependencies rarely change, so they're compiled once.

pitanja.pitanje: What can a $build.rs$ script do?
odgovori: Run after the tests finish to clean up
pitanja.zanimljivost: It prints instructions like $cargo:rerun-if-changed=…$ so Cargo knows when to run it again.

pitanja.pitanje: Why are mutually exclusive features discouraged?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Because of feature unification you can't control what others in the dependency graph turn on.

pitanja.pitanje: How does a user of this crate turn $json$ off?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Features are additive: Cargo unifies them across the whole dependency graph, so another crate can switch $json$ back on. That's why features should never remove functionality.

mediji.tekst:
[features]
default = ["json"]
json = ["dep:serde_json"]

pitanja.pitanje: What does $harness = false$ on a test target do?
odgovori: Tests run without any extra threads
pitanja.zanimljivost: Benchmark frameworks like $criterion$ use this to replace the built-in libtest harness.

pitanja.pitanje: Can integration tests use code behind $#[cfg(test)]$ in your library?
odgovori: No – the library is built without it
Yes – $cfg(test)$ is set for all test targets
pitanja.zanimljivost: $cfg(test)$ is set only when compiling the crate's own unit tests. Test helpers for others can go behind a feature instead.

pitanja.pitanje: Match each doc test annotation with its effect
pitanja.zanimljivost: $compile_fail$ is a cheap way to check that misuse of your API is rejected by the type system.

pitanja.pitanje: What is Miri?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Run with $cargo +nightly miri test$. It catches uninitialized reads, invalid pointers and aliasing violations.

pitanja.pitanje: What does the $loom$ crate do?
pitanja.zanimljivost: A loom (a weaving machine) weaves threads – it explores possible executions systematically, not just randomly.

pitanja.pitanje: What is fuzzing?
odgovori: Feeding random inputs to find crashes
Formatting source code automatically on save
pitanja.zanimljivost: $cargo-fuzz$ uses LLVM's libFuzzer, which watches code coverage and mutates inputs that reach new branches.

pitanja.pitanje: What do $proptest$ and $quickcheck$ do when they find a failing input?
odgovori: Shrink it to a minimal example
Save it as a new benchmark case
pitanja.zanimljivost: Instead of a 1000-element vector that fails, you get the smallest one that still fails.

pitanja.pitanje: Why do benchmarks use $std::hint::black_box$?
odgovori: To stop the optimizer removing work
To hide the benchmark's output from the user
pitanja.zanimljivost: If a result is never used, the compiler may delete the whole computation – and you'd benchmark nothing.

pitanja.pitanje: Without reflection-based mocking, how are dependencies usually mocked in Rust?
odgovori: Make code generic over a trait
pitanja.zanimljivost: Crates like $mockall$ generate the test implementations of such traits.

pitanja.pitanje: Why would you write a doc test with $compile_fail$ for a typestate API?
odgovori: To speed up the whole test suite
pitanja.zanimljivost: A plain test can only check what does compile – this checks what must not.

pitanja.pitanje: What runs the code in this comment?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Doc examples are compiled and run as tests, so documentation can't silently go stale. Lines starting with $# $ are hidden in the docs but still run.

pitanja.pitanje: What does hygiene mean for $macro_rules!$ macros?
odgovori: Macro locals don't clash with yours
It formats the code the macro produces
pitanja.zanimljivost: A variable declared inside a macro can't accidentally shadow or capture a variable at the call site.

pitanja.pitanje: Match each fragment specifier with what it matches
pitanja.zanimljivost: $tt$ is the most flexible – it matches almost anything, which makes it the building block of advanced macros.

pitanja.pitanje: In a $macro_rules!$ pattern, what does the repetition shown mean?
odgovori: Zero or more, separated by commas
pitanja.zanimljivost: $+$ means one or more, $?$ means zero or one.

pitanja.pitanje: Where must a procedural macro be defined?
odgovori: In any module of the crate that uses it
pitanja.zanimljivost: The compiler loads the macro crate as a plugin and runs it while compiling your crate.

pitanja.pitanje: What does a procedural macro receive and return?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Working with raw tokens keeps the compiler's internal syntax tree private, so it can change between versions.

pitanja.pitanje: Match each crate with its role in proc macros
pitanja.zanimljivost: $syn$ is one of the most downloaded crates on crates.io, because so many crates' derives depend on it.

pitanja.pitanje: What does $#[macro_export]$ do?
odgovori: Puts the macro at the crate root
Hides the macro from other crates' users
pitanja.zanimljivost: That's why exported macros are used as $mycrate::my_macro!$, no matter which module defined them.

pitanja.pitanje: Which tool shows the code after macros have expanded?
pitanja.zanimljivost: It's a separate tool ($cargo install cargo-expand$) and uses a nightly compiler feature under the hood.

pitanja.pitanje: Why prefer a declarative macro over a procedural one when either works?
odgovori: Declarative ones run at run time
pitanja.zanimljivost: Proc macros pull in $syn$ and friends, which must be compiled first – often the slowest part of a clean build.

pitanja.pitanje: What is the default recursion limit for macro expansion?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Recursive macros (e.g. tt-munchers) can hit it; $#![recursion_limit = "256"]$ raises it.

pitanja.pitanje: What does this print?
pitanja.zanimljivost: An $expr$ fragment is substituted as one parsed unit, as if wrapped in parentheses: $(2 + 1) * (2 + 1)$. The same C macro would give $2 + 1 * 2 + 1 = 5$.

pitanja.pitanje: What does $Future::poll$ return?
pitanja.zanimljivost: A future that returns $Pending$ promises it has arranged to be woken – otherwise it might never be polled again.

pitanja.pitanje: What is the $Waker$ in $Context$ for?
odgovori: Telling the executor to poll again
Waking up a sleeping OS thread directly
pitanja.zanimljivost: An I/O reactor stores the waker and calls $wake()$ when, for example, data arrives on a socket.

pitanja.pitanje: What does the compiler turn an $async fn$ into?
odgovori: A coroutine running on its own stack
pitanja.zanimljivost: Each $.await$ point is a state; local variables that live across it become fields of that state.

pitanja.pitanje: What does it mean that most types are $Unpin$?
odgovori: Pinning has no effect on them
pitanja.zanimljivost: Only types that may contain self-references (like compiler-generated futures) are $!Unpin$.

pitanja.pitanje: What does the reactor (I/O driver) in an async runtime do?
odgovori: Waits on OS events like epoll
Allocates memory for all the futures
pitanja.zanimljivost: The executor decides which task to poll next; the reactor tells it which tasks are ready.

pitanja.pitanje: Why does $tokio::spawn$ require a $Send + 'static$ future?
odgovori: The task may move between threads
All futures must live in the binary
pitanja.zanimljivost: A multi-threaded runtime steals tasks between worker threads to balance the load.

pitanja.pitanje: What goes wrong if a $std::sync::MutexGuard$ is held across $.await$?
odgovori: The guard is unlocked automatically at each $.await$
pitanja.zanimljivost: Either drop the guard before awaiting or use an async-aware mutex like $tokio::sync::Mutex$.

pitanja.pitanje: How do you cancel a future in Rust?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Code must be “cancellation safe”: a future can be dropped at any $.await$, e.g. when it loses a $select!$.

pitanja.pitanje: Why does a recursive $async fn$ need boxing?
odgovori: Its future would be infinitely large
pitanja.zanimljivost: Since Rust 1.77, a recursive call is allowed when the inner future is behind $Box::pin$.

pitanja.pitanje: What happens if one async task runs a long CPU loop without awaiting?
odgovori: The runtime preempts it after a time slice
It is moved to the GPU
pitanja.zanimljivost: Async scheduling is cooperative: a task yields only at $.await$. Tokio even adds a “budget” to force occasional yields.

pitanja.pitanje: Match each async building block with its role
pitanja.zanimljivost: With these four pieces you could write a tiny executor yourself – a classic exercise from the book.

pitanja.pitanje: About how long does this take?
pitanja.zanimljivost: $join!$ polls both futures in the same task, so their waiting overlaps. Writing $a.await; b.await;$ instead would take 2 seconds – the second future only starts after the first.

pitanja.pitanje: What does marking a function $unsafe fn$ signal?
odgovori: It runs without any bounds or borrow checks
pitanja.zanimljivost: An $unsafe$ block says “I checked”; an $unsafe fn$ says “you must check”. Since the 2024 edition, a lint asks for explicit $unsafe$ blocks inside it too.

pitanja.pitanje: What should a $// SAFETY:$ comment explain?
odgovori: How much faster it is than safe code
pitanja.zanimljivost: Clippy's $undocumented_unsafe_blocks$ lint can enforce that every $unsafe$ block has one.

pitanja.pitanje: Which of these is NOT undefined behavior?
pitanja.objasnjenje: Leaking is merely wasteful, not UB – $mem::forget$ is a safe function. The other three break the compiler's assumptions.
pitanja.zanimljivost: The compiler optimizes as if UB never happens, so UB can “travel backward” and break code that ran before it.

pitanja.pitanje: What type should you use for memory that's not initialized yet?
pitanja.zanimljivost: The old $mem::uninitialized$ is deprecated – it was UB for almost every type.

pitanja.pitanje: Why is creating a $bool$ from byte 2 immediate UB, while invalid UTF-8 in a $str$ isn't instantly UB?
odgovori: $str$ contents are checked at run time
pitanja.zanimljivost: The compiler relies on validity invariants (it may use the spare bit patterns of $bool$), while UTF-8 is a library promise that breaks only when something relies on it.

pitanja.pitanje: When is a safe API wrapping $unsafe$ code called sound?
odgovori: No safe use of it can cause UB
Miri hasn't complained about it yet
pitanja.zanimljivost: Soundness is about all possible callers, not just the ones you wrote.

pitanja.pitanje: Which of these traits requires $unsafe impl$?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Unsafe traits are ones where a wrong implementation can break memory safety elsewhere – $Send$, $Sync$, $GlobalAlloc$.

pitanja.pitanje: Why would a raw-pointer collection hold a $PhantomData<T>$ field?
odgovori: To force it onto the heap
pitanja.zanimljivost: It affects variance, auto traits and the drop check, which all look at fields – and a raw pointer alone says too little.

pitanja.pitanje: What does $NonNull<T>$ add over $*mut T$?
pitanja.zanimljivost: It's also covariant, and its niche lets $Option<NonNull<T>>$ be the size of a single pointer.

pitanja.pitanje: What must unsafe code consider about panics?
odgovori: Invariants must hold if one occurs
pitanja.zanimljivost: Example: calling $set_len$ before the elements are written – if a panic happens in between, $Drop$ sees garbage.

pitanja.pitanje: Which operation actually requires $unsafe$?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Making a raw pointer is safe – it's just a number. Only reading or writing through it is dangerous, because the compiler can't check that it points to valid memory. This prints 6.

pitanja.pitanje: Match each memory ordering with its guarantee
parovi: Later accesses stay after the load
Earlier accesses stay before the store
pitanja.zanimljivost: Rust's orderings come from the C++20 memory model. $Acquire$ and $Release$ come in pairs, like opening and closing a gate.

pitanja.pitanje: What does $AtomicUsize::fetch_add$ return?
pitanja.zanimljivost: The whole read-modify-write is one indivisible step, so two threads can't both read the same old value.

pitanja.pitanje: What does $compare_exchange(current, new, …)$ return when the value isn't $current$?
pitanja.zanimljivost: This is the basis of lock-free algorithms: read, compute, try to swap, and retry if someone else got there first.

pitanja.pitanje: In the actor model, how do actors share state?
odgovori: By passing $&mut$ references to each other
pitanja.zanimljivost: Each actor owns its state and processes one message at a time, so it needs no locks inside.

pitanja.pitanje: What is false sharing?
odgovori: Two atomics on one cache line
A data race in safe code
Cloning an $Arc$ too often in a hot loop
pitanja.zanimljivost: Cores keep stealing the same cache line from each other. $crossbeam$'s $CachePadded$ puts values on separate lines.

pitanja.pitanje: Which crate turns $.iter()$ into a parallel $.par_iter()$?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Rayon uses work stealing: idle threads take jobs from busy ones, so the work spreads evenly.

pitanja.pitanje: Which orderings does a simple spinlock typically use?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Spinlocks waste CPU while waiting; for most code a real $Mutex$, which puts threads to sleep, is better.

pitanja.pitanje: Why can't you just increment a $static mut$ counter from several threads?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Since the 2024 edition even creating a reference to a $static mut$ is an error by default.

pitanja.pitanje: What does $OnceLock$ provide?
odgovori: A mutex that only a single thread can use
pitanja.zanimljivost: Stabilized in Rust 1.70; $LazyLock$ (1.80) made the popular $lazy_static$ and $once_cell$ crates mostly unnecessary.

pitanja.pitanje: Why must code waiting on a $Condvar$ check its condition in a loop?
pitanja.zanimljivost: The OS may wake a thread even though nobody called $notify$, so the condition must be rechecked.

pitanja.pitanje: Does this compile, and what does it print?
pitanja.zanimljivost: A scope joins all its threads before returning, so they may borrow local data – even mutably, as long as only one thread does. Scoped threads came to the standard library in Rust 1.63.

pitanja.pitanje: What does $extern "C"$ on a function specify?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Rust's own calling convention is unspecified and can change between compiler versions.

pitanja.pitanje: Why add $#[no_mangle]$ to an exported function?
odgovori: To keep its symbol name as is
To make it safe to call
pitanja.zanimljivost: Rust normally mangles names (adds hashes) so different crates and versions don't collide. Since 2024 it's written $#[unsafe(no_mangle)]$.

pitanja.pitanje: Match each tool with its direction
pitanja.zanimljivost: $bindgen$ uses libclang to parse headers, so it understands macros and complex types well.

pitanja.pitanje: Which attribute should a struct passed to C have?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Without it Rust may reorder fields and C would read the wrong bytes.

pitanja.pitanje: Why can't you pass a $&str$ where C expects a $char*$ string?
odgovori: It can't be borrowed across the boundary
pitanja.zanimljivost: $CString$ owns a nul-terminated buffer; $CStr$ borrows one. Since 1.77 you can write literals like $c"hello"$.

pitanja.pitanje: Calling a function declared in an $extern$ block is…
pitanja.zanimljivost: The compiler can't check what foreign code does. Since 2024 you can write $unsafe extern$ and mark checked functions $safe$.

pitanja.pitanje: What happens since Rust 1.81 when a panic tries to unwind out of an $extern "C"$ function?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Unwinding into C used to be UB. If you really want it to cross the boundary, use the $"C-unwind"$ ABI.

pitanja.pitanje: How is a C type with hidden fields usually represented in Rust?
odgovori: An opaque struct you only point to
A $Vec<u8>$ copy of all of its fields
pitanja.zanimljivost: A common trick: $#[repr(C)] struct Handle { _private: [u8; 0] }$ plus a marker so it isn't $Send$ by accident.

pitanja.pitanje: How does C code usually pass state to a Rust callback?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Rust passes a pointer to its closure as $*mut c_void$ and a small $extern "C"$ trampoline casts it back.

pitanja.pitanje: What is the convention behind crates named $foo-sys$?
odgovori: Raw bindings; $foo$ is the safe wrapper
Deprecated old versions kept for compatibility
pitanja.zanimljivost: Only one crate in a build may link a given native library ($links = "foo"$), so splitting raw bindings out avoids conflicts.

pitanja.pitanje: How does a build script tell Cargo to link a native library?
pitanja.zanimljivost: $pkg-config$ and $cc$ crates help find and build C libraries from $build.rs$.

pitanja.pitanje: Why is the call wrapped in $unsafe$?
pitanja.zanimljivost: The compiler trusts the declared signature blindly – a wrong type there is undefined behaviour. Since the 2024 edition the block itself is $unsafe extern$; a function you know is harmless can be declared $safe fn$ and called without $unsafe$.

pitanja.pitanje: What remains available with $#![no_std]$?
odgovori: Threads and files, but no heap
pitanja.zanimljivost: $core$ has no allocation and no OS: $Option$, iterators, slices, formatting traits, atomics…

pitanja.pitanje: What does the $alloc$ crate add to a $no_std$ program?
odgovori: A garbage collector for the heap
pitanja.zanimljivost: You must also provide a $#[global_allocator]$ so it knows where to get memory.

pitanja.pitanje: What must a $no_std$ binary define that $std$ normally provides?
pitanja.zanimljivost: On a microcontroller the handler might blink an LED, write to a serial port, or just loop forever.

pitanja.pitanje: How do you choose the heap allocator for a whole program?
pitanja.zanimljivost: This also works with $std$ – e.g. to switch to $jemalloc$ or $mimalloc$.

pitanja.pitanje: Which of these is NOT available in $core$ alone?
pitanja.objasnjenje: $Vec$ needs heap allocation, so it lives in $alloc$ (and is re-exported by $std$).
pitanja.zanimljivost: The same $Option$ you use in $std$ is literally $core::option::Option$ re-exported.

pitanja.pitanje: On embedded targets, what does $#![no_main]$ allow?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Crates like $cortex-m-rt$ provide an $#[entry]$ attribute and set up the reset vector.

pitanja.pitanje: Why use $read_volatile$/$write_volatile$ for memory-mapped hardware registers?
odgovori: To lock the hardware while writing to it
pitanja.zanimljivost: Writing the same value twice to a register can matter to the hardware, even if the optimizer sees it as redundant.

pitanja.pitanje: What's a common pattern for libraries that work with or without $std$?
pitanja.zanimljivost: $#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "std"), no_std)]$ – $std$ is usually enabled by default.

pitanja.pitanje: Can you use $format!$ without an allocator?
odgovori: No – but $write!$ into a buffer works
Yes – it formats into a buffer on the stack
pitanja.zanimljivost: $format!$ returns a $String$. $core::fmt::Write$ lets you format into a fixed-size buffer.

pitanja.pitanje: Why must a $no_std$ binary write this function?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Without an operating system there's nobody to print a message and exit, so you decide: loop forever, reset the chip, blink an LED… The $!$ return type means the function never returns.

pitanja.pitanje: Clippy, Rust's linter, is named after…
pitanja.zanimljivost: It's named after the paper-clip assistant from old versions of Microsoft Office.

pitanja.pitanje: Match each tool with its job
pitanja.zanimljivost: All four ship as rustup components: $rustup component add clippy$.

pitanja.pitanje: What do $cargo-audit$ and $cargo-deny$ check?
odgovori: Code formatting against the style guide
pitanja.zanimljivost: They use the RustSec advisory database. $cargo-deny$ can also check licenses and duplicate versions.

pitanja.pitanje: How often is a new stable Rust released?
pitanja.zanimljivost: The “train” model: nightly → beta → stable. Features ready in time catch the next train.

pitanja.pitanje: Which Rust editions exist so far?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Crates of different editions work together in the same build – editions only change how one crate is parsed.

pitanja.pitanje: What is needed to use $#![feature(…)]$?
pitanja.zanimljivost: Unstable features can change or disappear, which is why stable Rust doesn't allow them.

pitanja.pitanje: How are big changes to Rust proposed and discussed?
odgovori: By a single maintainer who decides alone
pitanja.zanimljivost: RFC stands for “Request for Comments”; the process is public on GitHub in $rust-lang/rfcs$.

pitanja.pitanje: What does docs.rs do?
odgovori: Builds docs for every crate release
Tests every crate on all supported platforms
pitanja.zanimljivost: Every published version gets its own permanent documentation page.

pitanja.pitanje: Since Cargo 1.62, which command adds a dependency to $Cargo.toml$?
pitanja.zanimljivost: It used to be part of the $cargo-edit$ plugin. $cargo install$ is different – it installs binaries.

pitanja.pitanje: What is Crater?
odgovori: A tool that test-builds all public crates
A service that mirrors the crates.io registry
pitanja.zanimljivost: Before a release, the Rust team can build and test essentially every crate on crates.io with the old and new compiler.

pitanja.pitanje: Which versions may Cargo choose for this dependency?
pitanja.zanimljivost: A bare version is a caret requirement ($^1.0.150$): anything semver-compatible. Use $=1.0.150$ to pin it exactly – $Cargo.lock$ already pins it for applications.
